title.en: Distinguish fixed, programmable and flexible automation

say.en: A soap factory makes one shape of soap for years; a garment unit changes designs every season; a bank answers thousands of the same questions each day. Each needs a different kind of automation. In this lesson: Distinguish fixed, programmable and flexible automation.
Describe office and service automation.
Judge when automation is worthwhile.

body.en: Fixed (hard) *automation* uses equipment built for one fixed sequence of operations. It gives very high output at low unit cost, but is costly to set up and hard to change; it suits large volumes of a standard product. Programmable automation lets the sequence be changed by a new program; it suits batches of different products, with set-up time between batches. Flexible (soft) automation can switch between products quickly with little or no set-up time, as in computer-controlled machines and robots; it suits a variety of products in moderate volumes.

points.en: Fixed: one product, very high volume
Flexible: quick changeover, variety of products

body.en: Offices use *automation* to handle routine information work: automatic billing and reminders, payroll software, document scanning, e-mail filters, automated reports and software robots that copy data between systems. Services use ATMs, self check-in kiosks, online banking, chatbots and warehouse robots. Automation is worthwhile when volumes are high, tasks are repetitive and rule-based, accuracy matters, and the saving in running costs covers the cost of installing it.

points.en: Office: billing, payroll, reports, data entry by software
Pays off with high volume and routine, rule-based tasks

problem.en: A firm makes 60,000 units a year by hand at ₹30 a unit with a fixed cost of ₹3 lakh. A machine would cost ₹15 lakh a year (fixed) and ₹10 a unit. Should it automate now? What if sales double?

steps.en: At 60,000 units, both cost the same: 3 + 18 = ₹21 lakh and 15 + 6 = ₹21 lakh.
At 1,20,000 units: manual = 3 + 36 = ₹39 lakh; automated = 15 + 12 = ₹27 lakh.
Automation saves ₹12 lakh a year if sales double.

answer.en: At present volume it makes no difference; with doubled sales automation saves ₹12 lakh a year.

narration.en: Let us work this out step by step. A firm makes 60,000 units a year by hand at ₹30 a unit with a fixed cost of ₹3 lakh. A machine would cost ₹15 lakh a year (fixed) and ₹10 a unit. Should it automate now? What if sales double?

say.en: Let us work this out step by step. A firm makes 60,000 units a year by hand at 30 rupees a unit with a fixed cost of 3 rupees lakh. A machine would cost 15 rupees lakh a year fixed and 10 rupees a unit. Should it automate now? What if sales double?
Break-even volume equals (15,00,000 minus 3,00,000)/30 minus 10 equals 60,000 units.
At 60,000 units, both cost the same: 3 plus 18 equals 21 rupees lakh and 15 plus 6 equals 21 rupees lakh.
At 1,20,000 units: manual equals 3 plus 36 equals 39 rupees lakh; automated equals 15 plus 12 equals 27 rupees lakh.
Automation saves 12 rupees lakh a year if sales double.
So the answer is At present volume it makes no difference; with doubled sales automation saves 12 rupees lakh a year.

body.en: Fixed automation: huge volume, no variety. Flexible automation: variety, smaller volume. Programmable sits in between.
